value.overview: The Eastern Wood-Pewee (Contopus virens) is a small New World flycatcher that breeds in eastern and central North America and migrates to Central and northern South America. It is recognized by its subdued olive-gray plumage, two pale wing bars, peaked crown, and distinctive, plaintive “pee-a-wee” song. It usually hunts from exposed perches in forest edges, woodland clearings, shade plantations, and other habitats with scattered trees.
value.classification: The Eastern Wood-Pewee belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Contopus. It is closely related to the Western Wood-Pewee, but the two species have largely different breeding ranges and distinct calls.
value.identification: This is a slim, medium-small flycatcher with an olive-gray to brownish upper body, a dusky head, pale throat, and whitish or pale gray underparts. Two noticeable pale wing bars contrast with the dark wings, and the bill is broad and dark with a pale lower base. The tail is fairly long and dark. Its upright posture and habit of returning to the same perch are useful field marks. The clear, descending “pee-a-wee” song is often easier to recognize than the bird itself.
value.rangeHabitat: The Eastern Wood-Pewee breeds across much of eastern and central North America, using deciduous and mixed forests, woodland margins, parks, and forest openings. It migrates through Mexico and Central America to wintering areas in northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs as a seasonal migrant and winter visitor rather than a breeding species. It can be found in lowland and middle-elevation woodland, forest edges, open forest, gardens, and shaded agricultural landscapes, with numbers varying by season and location.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory. Eastern Wood-Pewees pass through Costa Rica during spring and fall migration, and some remain there during the northern winter. Costa Rica is outside the species’ breeding range; records are most likely from approximately September through April, although individual timing varies.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly from late spring through summer in North America. The species usually nests in a horizontal fork or on a small branch beneath the forest canopy, often in deciduous or mixed woodland. The female builds a small cup nest from plant fibers, grasses, and other material, commonly securing it with spider silk and decorating it with lichens. A typical clutch contains two or three eggs, and both adults participate in feeding the nestlings.
value.dietFeeding: The Eastern Wood-Pewee feeds mainly on flying insects, including moths, beetles, flies, wasps, bees, and other small arthropods. It usually hunts by sallying from a shaded perch, catching prey in the air, and returning to the same or a nearby perch. It may also take insects from vegetation and occasionally consume small fruits, especially when insects are less available.
value.behavior: This species is usually quiet outside the breeding season and often sits motionless on an exposed branch while scanning for prey. Its repeated flycatching sallies are short and direct. During the breeding season, adults defend territories with their characteristic song and may make short display flights. Migrants and wintering birds can occur alone or loosely associated with other insect-eating birds, but they generally retain separate feeding spaces.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is declining, largely because of reduced numbers across parts of its breeding range. The species remains widespread and relatively numerous.
conservation.threats: Potential concerns include loss and fragmentation of breeding and wintering forests, degradation of forest edges and shaded agricultural habitats, collisions during migration, and declines in flying insect abundance. Climate change may also alter migration timing, habitat conditions, and food availability.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native woodland in both breeding and wintering regions, retain mature trees and forest edges, and support shaded, pesticide-reduced agricultural systems. Reducing window collisions during migration and contributing observations to bird-monitoring programs can also help improve understanding of population changes.
